analysis.one_liner: Loosens post-2008 banking rules for smaller and midsize banks while adding credit-freeze and borrower protections.
analysis.headline: Became law in May 2018: the Senate passed it 67-31 and the House 258-159, freeing banks between $50 billion and $250 billion in assets from the strictest post-crisis oversight while adding free credit freezes and other consumer protections.
analysis.plain_summary: This law does two big things at once. It scales back rules Congress wrote after the 2008 financial crisis: most notably, banks with $50 billion to $250 billion in assets are no longer automatically subject to the strictest capital, stress-test, and supervision requirements, and small banks are exempted from rules like the Volcker Rule banning banks from trading for their own profit. It also adds consumer protections: credit bureaus must now provide free credit freezes, private student loan lenders can no longer demand payment when a cosigner dies or goes bankrupt, and renters in foreclosed buildings regained eviction protections that had lapsed.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and credit unions under $10 billion in assets get simplified capital rules, fewer reports, and exemptions from the Volcker Rule; banks between $50 billion and $250 billion get the single biggest win, escaping automatic application of the strictest post-crisis standards. Consumers get free credit freezes and longer fraud alerts, protections for private student loan cosigners and veterans' medical debt, and restored protections for renters in foreclosed properties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Community and midsize banks; credit consumers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the asset threshold for the strictest post-crisis bank standards from $50 billion to $250 billion, letting the Federal Reserve decide case by case which banks between $100 billion and $250 billion still face them

Exempts banks under $10 billion in assets from the Volcker Rule ban on trading for their own accounts, and creates a simplified capital ratio that counts as compliance with all other capital rules for community banks
Requires consumer reporting agencies to provide free credit freezes and longer fraud alerts, protections previously often available only for a fee

Bars private student loan creditors from declaring a default or accelerating the debt solely because a cosigner died or went bankrupt, and lets borrowers erase a reported default by completing a lender-run rehabilitation program
Restores the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, which had expired in 2014, giving renters in foreclosed properties back their notice and eviction protections
Limits the inclusion of veterans' medical debt in credit reports and makes permanent the one-year foreclosure grace period for servicemembers after leaving military service

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the trade-off in the other direction: oversight that was automatic for banks up to $250 billion now depends on regulators' discretion, mortgage-ability-to-repay standards are relaxed for loans small lenders keep on their books, public mortgage-lending data shrinks because smaller lenders are exempted from Home Mortgage Disclosure Act reporting, and physical inspections of small rural public housing agencies can drop to once every three years. Consumer reporting agencies lose the fees they used to charge for credit freezes.

drawbacks.text: Banks with $50 billion to $250 billion in assets are no longer automatically subject to the stricter capital, stress-test, and supervision standards put in place after the 2008 crisis, so regulators must instead decide which of these banks to oversee more closely

Smaller lenders can treat certain mortgages they keep on their books as qualified mortgages without meeting the full ability-to-repay standards, as long as they document the borrower's debt, income, and financial resources by a more flexible method

Lenders and credit unions originating fewer than 500 mortgages or 500 open-end credit lines per year are exempt from Home Mortgage Disclosure Act reporting requirements, shrinking the public data available on mortgage lending patterns
Small rural public housing agencies face physical inspections no more often than once every three years, and are exempt from environmental review for projects under $100,000

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections in Title III and Title VI are real and worth something to millions of people: free credit freezes became a nationwide right, student loan cosigners got genuine protection, and renters in foreclosed homes regained protections that had lapsed four years earlier. But the largest provisions by scale permanently lift the post-crisis oversight that applied to banks between $50 billion and $250 billion, and the bill relaxes several mortgage and lending standards whose risks fall on borrowers and the financial system rather than on the lenders. On balance, the bill's biggest and most permanent changes favor the banking industry, while the consumer benefits, though genuine, are narrower.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 67-31 on March 14, 2018; the House passed it 258-159 on May 22 under a rule that barred amendments; the President signed it on May 24, making it Public Law 115-174.

narrative.text: The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by the bill's sponsor, reported the bill with amendments in December 2017, and the Senate invoked cloture on the motion to proceed 67-32 before passing the amended bill 67-31, with Republicans voting 50-0 in favor and Democrats splitting 16-30
The House considered the Senate bill under a closed rule allowing no amendments and passed it 258-159, with Republicans voting 225-1 in favor and Democrats voting 33-158
The President signed the bill on May 24, 2018, and it became Public Law 115-174

The enacted law raises the enhanced-prudential-standards threshold from $50 billion to $250 billion, exempts banks under $10 billion from the Volcker Rule, requires free credit freezes, and restores the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks came out ahead: midsize banks between $50 billion and $250 billion in assets were permanently freed from automatic application of the strictest post-crisis standards, and community banks gained exemptions and simplified rules. Consumers gained too, most concretely through free credit freezes and student-loan cosigner protections, but the structural balance of the law tilts toward the industry.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Midsize and community banks; credit consumers

sides.party_line_note: Republicans backed it almost unanimously in both chambers (50 of 51 senators, 225 of 234 House members), while most Democrats opposed it (30 of 47 senators and 158 of 193 House members voted no), though a minority of Democrats crossed over in both chambers.

industries.industry: Midsize banks ($50 billion-$250 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill's headline provision raises the threshold for automatic strict oversight, stress tests, and risk committees from $50 billion to $250 billion, removing compliance costs for a set of large regional banks. The corresponding cost is borne broadly by the financial system and depositors, since oversight of these banks now rests on regulators' discretion rather than a fixed asset line.

industries.industry: Community banks and credit unions (under $10 billion)
industries.note: These lenders gain an exempted simplified capital ratio, exemption from the Volcker Rule, shorter examination cycles, reduced call reports, and the ability to treat certain held mortgages as qualified without the full ability-to-repay standard. Supporters argue this lowers credit costs for borrowers; loosened underwriting standards shift the risk of unsuitable loans to consumers.

The bill requires agencies to provide credit freezes free of charge, end credits the industry previously billed consumers for, and extend fraud alert durations. Their revenue loss is consumers' direct gain.

Lenders lose the ability to accelerate loans or declare default solely because a cosigner died or went bankrupt, and must offer rehabilitation programs that erase reported defaults. Borrowers and cosigners gain protections they previously lacked.

Qualifying retailers of manufactured and modular homes are generally excluded from the definition of mortgage originator under the Truth in Lending Act, easing their financing arrangements. Buyers gain access to financing but with lighter disclosure and originator requirements.
